sections.h2: What is a lady bird deed in Michigan?
sections.html:
It is a deed in which the owner keeps a life estate and full power to sell, mortgage, or lease the home, while naming someone who receives it at the owner's death. Michigan's Department of Health and Human Services defines it in its Bridges policy glossary as an enhanced life estate deed, also called a transfer on death deed, that lets property pass on death without probate. The owner still owns the property and can sell, rent, or change it without restriction until death.

Michigan Treasury uses nearly the same picture in its principal residence exemption guidance. Its example has an owner deed the home to another person while reserving a life estate and full power to convey during life, including selling, gifting, mortgaging, leasing, or keeping the proceeds. Treasury names that arrangement a Lady Bird Deed.

The instrument still has to be a valid Michigan deed. The statutory short form for a quitclaim says a conveyance worded in substance as a quitclaim, signed, sealed, and acknowledged by the grantor, is a good conveyance to the grantee and the grantee's heirs and assigns (MCL 565.152). That form does not by itself describe a retained life estate, so the wording of the retained powers is what a Michigan attorney will draft.

sections.h2: How does the Michigan Medicaid program treat the deed?
sections.html:
Two different rules are in play, and both come from the state agency. On eligibility, the glossary says that because the grantor keeps unrestricted interest in the property, a lady bird deed is not considered a divestment when an applicant is in a divestment penalty situation.

Estate recovery is a separate question. MDHHS says it applies to Medicaid beneficiaries who are 55 or older and received long-term care services on or after September 30, 2007. The agency defines the estate as property passing to heirs through probate, but for someone who received an asset disregard from a long-term care partnership policy, recovery applies to all assets whether or not they pass through probate (MDHHS Estate Recovery).

The agency also defers recovery while a spouse, a child under 21, or a blind or permanently disabled child is living. An undue hardship waiver is possible for a home of modest value, meaning one worth less than 50% of the average home price in its county on the date of death, and the applicant must pass a means test of household income under 200% of the poverty level and household resources under $10,000.

MDHHS also warns that transferring assets to avoid recovery can affect eligibility, and that the law presumes no undue hardship when the hardship results from such a transfer (MCL 400.112g(3)(e)(iii)). Speak with a legal advisor before you sign a deed with Medicaid in mind.

sections.h2: Does a lady bird deed change the property tax exemption or taxable value?
sections.html:
It can affect who qualifies for the principal residence exemption. Treasury says a person who holds a life estate counts as a partial owner and is eligible if the home is their principal residence, and that any ownership interest must be in writing. In Treasury's lady bird example, the person named to receive the home has no current ownership interest because the grantor keeps full control, and becomes an owner only at the grantor's death if the grantor has not used the powers.

Taxable value is a separate issue. Under MCL 211.27a, a transfer of ownership uncaps taxable value in the year after the transfer. Subsection (6) defines transfer of ownership broadly, and subsection (7) lists transfers that are exempt from that definition. Treasury's change-of-ownership page says a transfer of ownership causes uncapping in the calendar year following the year of the transfer. Whether a particular deed, or the later death of the grantor, counts is a question for the local assessor.

sections.h2: Can I still sell a Michigan house that has a lady bird deed?
sections.html:
If the deed keeps the full powers described above, the grantor is the person who sells. The MDHHS glossary says the owner may sell or rent without restriction until death, and Treasury's example lists selling, gifting, mortgaging, and leasing among the retained powers. A buyer's title company will still want to read the recorded deed itself, because a deed written with narrower powers changes who must sign.

  • Pull the recorded deed from the county register of deeds and read the retained powers.
  • Ask the title company whether it needs the named recipient's signature or a release.
  • If the grantor has died, the deed that names the recipient is the starting point, and the recipient should ask the assessor and the title company how the transfer is handled.

Michigan's simplified affidavit for small estates, court form PC 598, can be used only when no real property is in the decedent's estate, so a house is not handled through that form.

sections.h2: What happens to the exemption and taxes when the owner dies?
sections.html:
Treasury's claim guidance says a deceased owner is no longer eligible because the owner cannot occupy the home or intend to return. The estate's personal representative or trustee must file Form 2602, the Request to Rescind Principal Residence Exemption, with the assessor within 90 days of death. The exemption is removed as of December 31 of the year the rescission was filed.

The person who receives the home and lives there can claim a new exemption by filing Form 2368 with the assessor if they meet the ownership rules, by June 1 for the summer levy or November 1 for the winter levy (MCL 211.7cc(2)). A property transfer affidavit may also be needed, so ask the local assessor which filings apply to a transfer at death.

sections.h2: What should an owner ask before signing a lady bird deed?
sections.html:
The deed is a recorded legal document, and small wording differences control who owns what. Bring these questions to a Michigan attorney.

  • Which powers does the deed reserve: selling, mortgaging, leasing, and gifting?
  • Does the owner want a Medicaid planning result, and how does estate recovery apply if there is a long-term care partnership policy?
  • How will the county assessor treat the deed for uncapping and the principal residence exemption?
  • Who will file the rescission and affidavit forms after death, and within what time?

Call the assessor for the city or township where the home sits, and the register of deeds for the county, for their recording and filing requirements.

faqs.q: Does Michigan call it a lady bird deed in its official materials?
faqs.a: Yes, in two places. The MDHHS Bridges policy glossary lists Lady Bird Deed as another name for an enhanced life estate deed or transfer on death deed, and Treasury's exemption guidance uses the term in an ownership example.

faqs.q: Is a lady bird deed a Medicaid divestment in Michigan?
faqs.a: No, according to the MDHHS glossary. Because the grantor keeps unrestricted interest in the property, the deed is not considered a divestment when an applicant is in a divestment penalty situation.

faqs.q: Does the deed avoid Medicaid estate recovery?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. MDHHS says recovery reaches all assets, probate or not, for beneficiaries who received an asset disregard under a long-term care partnership policy, so ask a legal advisor how your facts apply.

faqs.q: Can the person named in the deed claim the principal residence exemption?
faqs.a: Not while the grantor keeps full control. Treasury says that person has no current ownership interest and becomes an owner only at the grantor's death if the powers were not used.

faqs.q: Does recording a lady bird deed raise property taxes?
faqs.a: That depends on whether the conveyance is a transfer of ownership under MCL 211.27a. A transfer of ownership uncaps taxable value in the next calendar year, so ask the local assessor before you record.
